Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

AI.tldr: Safe Personal RSI evaluates and repairs prompt-level self-improvement updates for the Kicker personal health assistant, rejecting unsafe edits before deployment.
AI.motivation: Updating reusable instructions in personal assistants can improve task handling but also alter what the assistant discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions, creating safety and authorization risks.
AI.method: Restricting recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates with fixed weights and runtime code, the procedure tests proposed and current instructions on a 29-case executable benchmark (covering email, calendar, health, marketplace, and injection probes), temporarily reverts failing changes to guide repairs, and adopts updates only if safety and task checks pass.
AI.result: Across three models and two risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts; a GPT-5.6 Luna repair cuts attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and raises safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%, while a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and raises safe completion from 19.5% to 64.4%.
AI.conclusion: Automated pre-adoption testing and revert-guided repair can block unsafe prompt updates and improve attack resistance in personal agents, while runtime probes also expose underlying OAuth scope gaps.

title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

AI.tldr: Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD) distills a black-box teacher's capabilities into a smaller student agent using natural-language adviser interactions rather than teacher logits.
AI.motivation: Conventional on-policy distillation improves agents on long-horizon tasks but requires access to teacher token logits, which text-only black-box frontier models do not expose.
AI.method: During execution, the student autonomously decides when to query a black-box teacher with open-ended natural-language requests; successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts via on-policy self-distillation combined with task-reward RL.
AI.result: On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46x the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline, and the learned capabilities generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2 without adviser access at test time.
AI.conclusion: Natural-language consultation paired with on-policy self-distillation offers an effective alternative to logit-based distillation for transferring black-box teacher capabilities to smaller long-horizon agents.

title: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
comment: 34 pages, 11 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $\tau^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($\tau^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates overnight LoRA fine-tuning of small on-device models from user reactions over simulated year-long deployments, finding that learning holds up only when the judge filters out failures and the user can see the true outcome.
AI.motivation: Small on-device language models could improve overnight from daily interactions, but without ground-truth outcomes, both self-judgment and noisy user reactions can mislead learning.
AI.method: The authors fine-tune Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B models with LoRA each night on judge-accepted attempts across 127 simulated lives (up to one year) on WebShop and tau^2-bench, comparing true outcomes, user verdicts, model self-judgment, and three versions of a frozen "feedback sense" that interprets user reactions.
AI.result: Self-judging models consistently improved initially and then decayed; a naive feedback sense collapsed in 3 of 5 lives, whereas a discernment-based sense kept 4 of 5 lives near oracle performance for two weeks before fading by day 60. On tau^2-bench where users cannot see outcomes, 80% of accepted lessons were thanked failures, and across 97 lives the share of failed lessons strongly predicted decay (Spearman rho = -0.81).
AI.conclusion: Continual on-device learning from user feedback is viable only when users can observe task outcomes and the feedback filter reliably excludes failed attempts.

title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

AI.tldr: AnyS1 mines enumerable decision points from public procedural skills to train a single 4B System-1 model that resolves routine agent decisions in one pass, cutting cost and latency across unseen benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Autonomous LLM agents waste cost and latency by calling large System-2 models at every step, even for routine choices among small candidate sets, while existing dual-system approaches require hand-authored, workflow-specific hooks.
AI.method: AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions from over 1,000 public procedural skills, collects execution-grounded trajectory states in isolated containers (Any-DP), and trains a calibrated 4B pointer System-1 model with label smoothing that handles routine choices at runtime and falls back to System-2 below a confidence threshold.
AI.result: Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while reducing episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, including under zero-shot threshold transfer.
AI.conclusion: Public procedural skills provide a domain-general source of decision points for training a single reusable System-1 model that substantially reduces agent inference cost and latency.

title: Geometry-bridge flow matching for blind rigid-motion correction in head cone-beam CT
summary: Rigid motion of a patient head during head cone-beam CT (CBCT) scan can degrade image quality and complicate recovery of accurate anatomical structures from the measured projections. We present a 3D flow-matching prior approach that learns the image changes induced by motion. Its geometry-bridge connects motion-corrupted and motion-free Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructed images of the same source volume through progressively reduced simulated motion. The forward projector's geometry derivative supplies analytic velocity targets along this path. A plug-and-play loop encompasses the learned image updates together with spline-based pose estimation, conjugate-gradient data consistency, and image total-variation regularization. Both the refined image volume and the FDK reconstructed image volume at the estimated poses are evaluated. On simulated 360-view scans from 30 held-out CQ500 patients with nominal per-component motion amplitudes within 10 mm / 10 degrees, the framework achieved state-of-the-art image reconstruction quality and motion accuracy in comparison with other methos such as learned autofocus and diffusion-based joint reconstruction. Mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) reached 37.1 dB and mean detector-plane reprojection error (RPE) was 0.27 mm. With matched endpoints at the inference settings, the geometry bridge improved PSNR by 1.6 dB and reduced RPE by 33% relative to image-linear training. With 50 prior updates and coarse-to-fine motion estimation, total processing time averaged 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a 3D geometry-bridge flow-matching prior for blind rigid-motion correction in head cone-beam CT, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction quality and pose accuracy.
AI.motivation: Rigid patient head motion during cone-beam CT scans degrades image quality and complicates anatomical recovery from measured projections.
AI.method: A 3D flow-matching prior learns image changes along a geometry-bridge connecting motion-corrupted and motion-free FDK reconstructions via progressively reduced simulated motion and analytic velocity targets from the forward projector's geometry derivative, embedded in a plug-and-play loop with spline pose estimation, conjugate-gradient data consistency, and total-variation regularization.
AI.result: On simulated 360-view scans from 30 held-out CQ500 patients with motion within 10 mm and 10 degrees, the framework achieves 37.1 dB mean PSNR and 0.27 mm mean detector-plane reprojection error, outperforming learned autofocus and diffusion baselines and improving PSNR by 1.6 dB (33% lower RPE) over image-linear training at 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.
AI.conclusion: Grounding flow-matching priors in projector geometry derivatives provides an effective plug-and-play solution for blind rigid-motion correction in head CBCT.

title: Sightline: Long-Window Speculative Decoding for Fast SVG Generation
comment: 45 pages, 23 figures, 34 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation models write a graphic as code with one forward pass per token, so drawing is slow. Speculative decoding speeds them up losslessly, and block drafters guess many tokens per pass. On SVG, many of their rounds accept the whole draft and end only at the verification window. We find that their misses are rare and clumped, and that they stay accurate far deeper into a block than on natural language. A run-length identity and three propositions show that a longer window pays once the candidates are wide, up to the drafter's horizon. We propose Sightline, which pairs a window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Experiments cover text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG with three models on six benchmarks from MMSVG, MMSVG-2M and SArena. In every setting, Sightline is the fastest of the compared lossless decoders. On SArena, it stays the fastest when every decoder shares one loop control. It also leads in almost every setting of six models from four other families, which write SVG code, compressed SVG tokens or Lottie JSON. Analyses trace the lead to rounds that shorter windows cut off, both in loop-free content and in loops. Speculative decoding also saves time for choosing samples by rendering, which beats choosing by likelihood. These results suggest that speculative decoding on vector graphics should verify as far as the drafter sees. Code and data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Sightline accelerates lossless speculative decoding for SVG generation by pairing a long verification window matched to the drafter's horizon with a wide draft tree.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive SVG generation is slow token-by-token, and standard block-drafter speculative decoding often accepts entire drafts up to short verification windows because SVG misses are rare and clumped.
AI.method: Guided by a run-length identity showing longer windows pay off once candidates are wide enough, Sightline sets the verification window equal to the drafter's full horizon and pairs it with a wide draft tree.
AI.result: Across text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG on six benchmarks (MMSVG, MMSVG-2M, SArena) and nine models spanning SVG code, compressed tokens, and Lottie JSON, Sightline is the fastest lossless decoder in every setting and also speeds up render-based sample selection.
AI.conclusion: Because vector-graphics drafters remain accurate much deeper into a block than in natural language, speculative decoding for SVG should verify across the drafter's entire horizon.

title: A System 1 Decision Model for Medical Multiple-Choice Questions Built on Frozen Language Models
summary: A System 1 model answers a multiple-choice question in a single pass. A frozen language model turns the question and each option into vectors, two small, trained heads place them in a shared space, and the closest option wins. The design has been shown on agent decisions, but we are not aware of a study of how far it goes on exam questions that need medical knowledge, where the right option is often no more similar to the question than the wrong ones. We rebuilt the recipe from scratch for MedMCQA and trained only two projection heads and one temperature on top of frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, Granite-4.2-3B and Qwen3-8B, using a contrastive loss with in-batch and hard negatives and a mask for repeated answers. With plain last-token vectors, both small encoders answer about one question in three correctly (33.1% and 33.0% on 3,842 held-out questions, where chance is 25.0%). Writing each text inside a one-word-summary prompt and lowering the learning rate of the heads raised this to 41.7% and 42.5% for the two small encoders and to 46.0% +-0.2 (three seeds) for Qwen3-8B. Shuffling the questions against the options returns accuracy to chance, so the heads do use the question. Flan-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2 report 57.6% and 72.3% on MedMCQA under a different protocol, so ours is a cheap, fast baseline and not a competitive system. We also say what our evidence cannot show: validation gains were about 1.7 to 2 times the test gains, and we could not separate the effect of reading several encoder layers from the other changes.

AI.tldr: This paper tests how far a single-pass System 1 model built on frozen LLMs with trained projection heads can go on medical multiple-choice questions in MedMCQA.
AI.motivation: Single-pass System 1 vector-matching models have been demonstrated on agent decisions, but their effectiveness on knowledge-intensive medical exams where correct options are not lexically similar to questions was unknown.
AI.method: Two small projection heads and a temperature parameter are trained on top of frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, Granite-4.2-3B, and Qwen3-8B using a contrastive loss with in-batch and hard negatives, repeated-answer masking, and a one-word-summary prompt.
AI.result: On 3,842 held-out MedMCQA questions (chance 25.0%), plain last-token vectors yield 33.1% and 33.0% for the small encoders, while one-word-summary prompting and lower head learning rates raise accuracy to 41.7%, 42.5%, and 46.0% +/- 0.2 for Qwen3-8B (compared to 57.6% for Flan-PaLM and 72.3% for Med-PaLM 2 under different protocols).
AI.conclusion: Frozen-LLM System 1 projection heads provide a fast, low-cost baseline for medical multiple-choice questions that genuinely uses question-option matching, though they remain well below full fine-tuned or large medical models.

title: Rethinking Fixed-Horizon Latent Reasoning
summary: Existing latent reasoners typically run for a preset latent horizon during inference. Intuitively, a longer horizon should provide more opportunity for reasoning. However, in this work, we find that extending latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) to the full preset horizon may in fact degrade reasoning performance. We observe that latent CoT evolves through distinct functional stages, with earlier computation forming frontier reasoning states, while later computation mainly reorganizes existing candidates and can weaken gold candidate support. These findings motivate a rethink of fixed-horizon latent inference. To address this, we characterize the reasoning benefits of latent CoT by realized and remaining constructive progress. Empirically, we find that higher realized constructive progress corresponds to higher current reasoning accuracy, while more remaining progress corresponds to larger future gains from continued latent CoT. To this end, we introduce a lightweight method that estimates the remaining reasoning progress and adaptively adjusts the latent horizon during inference. Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, our method improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0%, without retraining the LLM.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that running latent Chain-of-Thought to a fixed preset horizon can degrade reasoning accuracy and proposes an adaptive horizon-stopping method based on remaining constructive progress.
AI.motivation: Latent reasoners typically execute for a fixed number of steps at inference, but later computation often reorganizes existing candidates and weakens support for the gold answer rather than improving reasoning.
AI.method: The authors characterize latent CoT via realized and remaining constructive progress and introduce a lightweight, training-free inference method that estimates remaining progress to adaptively adjust the latent horizon.
AI.result: Across representative latent CoT reasoners and multiple arithmetic benchmarks, adaptive horizon control improves reasoning accuracy by up to 7.2 percentage points while reducing latent computation by up to 29.0% without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Estimating remaining constructive progress during latent reasoning prevents late-stage degradation and simultaneously improves accuracy and efficiency.

title: Measuring and Charging for Retained Context in Long-Context LLM Services
comment: 33 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables, including Appendices A-F; code and recorded data included as ancillary material
summary: Long-context large language model (LLM) services charge for repeated context, yet billing weights need not reflect its contribution to answer quality. We present a three-layer framework separating content relevance, observable proxies and auditable positional weights. Context-ablation experiments show that relevance dominates position and that distance-decay families do not outperform a relevance-only baseline. A measured serving stack shows that cache hits reduce repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens, while cold resends constrain sustainable discounts. Cross-provider measurements separate cache value from tokenisation and list-price differences. Calibrated simulations reduce the 99th percentile of session charges by 31-42%, although revenue-matched nonlinear tariffs achieve similar reductions and median charges increase. The framework provides a bounded per-token accounting rule and measured deployment constraints, rather than a validated utility estimator.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a three-layer framework for measuring and billing retained context in long-context LLM services, finding that content relevance dominates token position.
AI.motivation: Long-context LLM services charge for repeated context, yet existing billing weights do not necessarily reflect how much retained tokens actually contribute to answer quality.
AI.method: The authors separate content relevance, observable proxies, and auditable positional weights, combining context-ablation experiments, serving-stack cache measurements, cross-provider comparisons, and calibrated tariff simulations.
AI.result: Ablations show relevance dominates position and distance-decay models do not beat a relevance-only baseline; cache hits cut repeated-prefix compute cost by over two orders of magnitude at 65,536 tokens while cold resends limit discounts; calibrated simulations reduce 99th-percentile session charges by 31-42% (though median charges rise).
AI.conclusion: The framework establishes a bounded per-token accounting rule and deployment constraints for long-context billing rather than a validated utility estimator.

title: Meaning Reaches Object Choice but Not Completion: Where Is a VLA Vulnerable to Landmark Synonyms?
comment: Accepted to the CoRL 2026 Workshop on The Action Gap (TAG 2026). OpenReview: this https URL
summary: VLA policies are fragile to rewording. Success rates alone cannot say whether a policy fails to choose the object or to complete the task, nor where in the policy to intervene. We study the released GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to take. Synonyms absent from the training instructions send the policy to the bowl they name, unlike made-up words, yet complete 67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes, against the original word's 100%. Before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator, replacing only the landmark tokens' vectors with the other landmark's (pasting) sends nearly every episode to the other bowl. After the connector, pasting at the landmark, the remaining instruction, or the image tokens alone rarely moves the choice, but any two do. Hiding the landmark tokens from the action generator after the connector still lowers completion for the synonyms that fall short. Finetuning on diversified landmark words repairs that one task's completion for synonyms absent from finetuning; finetuning on the original instructions does not. Training only the connector on the diversified words suffices, as does copying the connector of a policy fully finetuned on them into one finetuned on the original instructions. An open-loop score on starting frames misses that weights outside the connector also carry part of the repair. For now, on this evidence, robustness to rewording should be judged in closed loop, with actions executed, intervening on both sides of the connector, scoring choice and completion separately.

AI.tldr: This paper localizes where vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail on reworded instructions, showing that landmark synonyms reach the right object but fail during task completion unless the connector is adapted.
AI.motivation: Success rates alone cannot distinguish whether a VLA policy fails to select the target object or fails to complete the manipulation when instructions are reworded, nor where to intervene in the architecture.
AI.method: Using GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in a landmark word, the authors perform closed-loop activation pasting before and after the VLM-to-action connector, token masking, and targeted finetuning on diversified landmark words.
AI.result: Unseen synonyms route the policy to the named bowl but complete only 67.6% of closed-loop episodes (versus 100% for the original word); pasting landmark vectors before the connector flips object choice, whereas after the connector two token groups must be pasted; finetuning only the connector on diversified words restores completion for unseen synonyms.
AI.conclusion: Rewording robustness in VLAs must be evaluated in closed loop with separate choice and completion metrics, as the VLM-to-action connector is a primary bottleneck for completion under synonym shifts.

title: Constructing Dynamic Conversations with Neural Back-channel Generation and Voice-line Scheduling
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, project page this https URL
summary: We present a novel approach to the problem of combining two voice-line channels of dyadic conversational audio into a unified conversation with controllable back-channeling and turn-taking dynamics. In voice performances for the game industry, the two tracks of voice-lines are typically recorded or synthesized in isolation. Our method takes two such unsynchronized tracks and uses a neural scheduler to sequence them into a single dynamic conversation, modifying both tracks by inserting or removing pauses and introducing voice overlap as appropriate. We further propose a back-channel predictor that is able to predict opportunity for back-channels for a given conversational turn's audio and content, which the scheduler can then incorporate. We evaluate our scheduler and predictor independently and in combination by: various quantitative comparison; a qualitative and perceptual comparison to prior art and naive baselines; a compelling set of results showing animator control over the diversity, extent and nature of back-channeling and turn dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a neural scheduling and back-channel prediction system that merges two isolated voice-line tracks into a natural, controllable dyadic conversation.
AI.motivation: In game voice production, two conversational tracks are typically recorded or synthesized in isolation, lacking synchronized turn-taking, pauses, overlaps, and back-channeling.
AI.method: A neural scheduler sequences two unsynchronized voice-line tracks by inserting or removing pauses and introducing overlaps, guided by a back-channel predictor that forecasts back-channel opportunities from each turn's audio and content.
AI.result: Quantitative comparisons, perceptual evaluations against prior art and naive baselines, and qualitative demonstrations show improved conversational naturalness and animator control over back-channeling and turn-taking dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Combining neural voice-line scheduling with content- and audio-aware back-channel prediction enables controllable synthesis of dynamic conversations from isolated recordings.

title: From a finite subgroup of $SO(3)$:$C_2$ leads to a Holant dichotomy
summary: Counting complexity within the Holant framework has been extensively studied through complexity dichotomy theorems. While substantial progress has been achieved for various restricted settings, the general complex-valued even-arity case without auxiliary unary signatures remains largely open. This paper studies a fundamental case in this program where the binary signatures induce a group structure satisfying \(M(B(\mathcal{F}))\cong C_2\). It is observed that projective equivalence classes of binary signature matrices naturally embed into finite subgroups of \(SO(3)\), providing an algebraic viewpoint for structural classification. This paper further identifies two fundamentally different regimes for the \(C_2\) case, namely the normal and isotropic cases, and analyzes their complexity behavior separately. Combining gadget constructions, decomposition techniques, interpolation arguments, and a realnumberization approach that transforms the complex-valued setting into an equivalent real-structured framework, this paper establishes a complete dichotomy theorem: for every even-arity signature set \(\mathcal{F}\) satisfying \(M(\B(\mathcal{F}))\cong C_2\), the problem \(\mathrm{Holant}(\mathcal{F})\) is either polynomial-time computable or \#P-hard. A Pauli-basis representation for signatures is further introduced as an algebraically natural language for organizing realizable signatures and revealing structural relations that are less transparent in the standard basis.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes a complete complexity dichotomy for complex-valued even-arity Holant problems whose binary signatures generate a C_2 group structure.
AI.motivation: While Holant complexity dichotomies exist for restricted settings, the general complex-valued even-arity case without auxiliary unary signatures remains largely open.
AI.method: Exploiting the embedding of projective binary signature classes into finite subgroups of SO(3), the authors separate the C_2 case into normal and isotropic regimes and combine gadget constructions, decomposition, interpolation, realnumberization, and a Pauli-basis signature representation.
AI.result: The authors prove a complete dichotomy theorem showing that for every even-arity signature set F with M(B(F)) isomorphic to C_2, Holant(F) is either polynomial-time computable or #P-hard.
AI.conclusion: Viewing binary signatures through finite subgroups of SO(3) and the Pauli basis provides an effective algebraic framework for resolving open complex-valued Holant dichotomies.

title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
summary: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.

AI.tldr: MoE-Context splits agent history into blocks and uses a fast pass to mask unneeded blocks into one-line notes over a single KV cache, boosting lookup accuracy while revealing that model-based block selection remains the weak link.
AI.motivation: AI agents typically re-read their entire history at every step, whereas keeping only immediately relevant context active with lightweight recall notes could improve accuracy and efficiency.
AI.method: Context is partitioned into blocks; before each step a fast yes/no pass selects needed blocks while others remain as one-line recallable notes, implemented by masking hidden blocks in a single KV cache without deleting them.
AI.result: On a synthetic lookup task with Qwen3-1.7B, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a supervised linear probe lifts the model's own block-picking accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, though simple keyword search is perfect on this task and the probe does not transfer to a second task.
AI.conclusion: Masking irrelevant context blocks in a shared KV cache substantially improves answer accuracy and enables cheap undo and subagent patterns, provided a reliable block-selection mechanism is used.

title: Transferring an analysis of human brain organization to language models
comment: 5 figures, 5 extended data figures, 5 extended data tables; includes Supplementary Information
summary: During human cortical development, functional systems become increasingly differentiated. We asked whether improved reasoning in language models involves a comparable regional reorganization. Applying diffusion-map embedding, used to characterize cortical organization, to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families, we found broadly preserved gradient profiles with localized changes within a contiguous layer span. Grafting weights from these spans into instruction-tuned hosts improved mathematical reasoning on average, with gains rising with region overlap, while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere. Across training, the span formed gradually during the early rise in performance, and grafts from intermediate stages helped. Grafts shifted most hosts partly towards their donors' behaviour and sometimes improved on problems the donors failed; the same analysis located a transferable span in a medical model. Together, these findings identify a reasoning-related region whose weights improve reasoning with low interference in the host's existing mathematical competence.

AI.tldr: Applying cortical diffusion-map embedding to language models reveals a localized, contiguous layer span whose weights transfer mathematical reasoning ability to instruction-tuned hosts with low interference.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether reasoning training in language models induces localized functional reorganization analogous to cortical differentiation in human brain development.
AI.method: The authors apply diffusion-map embedding to matched base and reasoning-trained models from three families to locate shifted layer spans, then graft those weight spans into instruction-tuned host models and evaluate mathematical reasoning and retention.
AI.result: Gradient profiles are broadly preserved with localized changes in a contiguous layer span; grafting these spans improves mathematical reasoning on average (scaling with region overlap) while retaining more previously solved problems than grafts elsewhere, and the same analysis identifies a transferable span in a medical model.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning training induces a localized, transferable weight region in language models that can boost reasoning in host models with minimal disruption to existing competence.

title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
summary: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference this http URL apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2,000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical this http URL discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

AI.tldr: Applying PPO with LoRA and a simple length- and punctuation-based self-supervised reward to Mistral-7B produces longer, better-structured medical explanations without human preference labels.
AI.motivation: Small language models suited for on-premises clinical deployment often generate short, poorly structured medical explanations, and supervised CoT distillation does not explicitly optimize rationale organization.
AI.method: Building on Mistral-7B, the authors run ~170 steps of PPO with LoRA on 2,000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts using a self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones.
AI.result: Training on a single A100 GPU yields a stable reward increase, and quantitative and qualitative evaluations show longer, more organized multi-point explanations that preserve underlying medical content.
AI.conclusion: Lightweight self-rewarded RL can effectively shape the structure and readability of medical rationales in small language models without human preference data.

title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
comment: 41 pages. Ancillary files: a public sample of 48 development instances with scripted-oracle episodes. Hosted evaluation: this https URL
summary: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

AI.tldr: Openhagen Worlds is a calibrated suite of 27 procedurally generated scientific discovery environments designed to separate genuine experimental reasoning from recall and shortcut policies.
AI.motivation: Existing scientific discovery benchmarks often conflate experimental reasoning with memorization, unstated scoring rules, or exploitable shortcuts.
AI.method: The suite comprises 27 procedural environments (178 calibrated difficulty levels across 92 core and 86 frontier rungs) where agents run budgeted experiments and submit answers to a deterministic verifier, with each level admitted only if a scripted oracle scores >=0.75, the strongest non-deductive policy <=0.25, and gated shortcuts <=0.35 on 64 dev instances.
AI.result: On 84 withheld frontier instances, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at default effort (16,384 tokens/call) and 57 at maximum effort (up to 393,216 tokens/call) versus 79 for the oracle, while on-policy expert iteration raises a 9B model's core-tier success from 0.090 to 0.148 with no loss on GPQA Diamond.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated, shortcut-gated environments provide a rigorous testbed for measuring and training multi-stage scientific discovery agents.

title: DRIFT: Detachable Reasoning for Runtime-Flexible and Efficient End-to-End Driving
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance. With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: DRIFT is a 255M-parameter end-to-end autonomous driving framework that distills a lightweight LM into surrogate reasoning features so language reasoning can be toggled off at runtime without hurting driving performance.
AI.motivation: Integrating VLMs into end-to-end driving aids scene reasoning but is computationally expensive, and prior systems cannot switch language reasoning on and off at runtime without degrading closed-loop performance.
AI.method: DRIFT projects intermediate driving representations into a <150M-parameter LM for VQA and commentary, and trains a runtime-flexible planning module on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM so inference can condition on either the LM or the surrogate features.
AI.result: On Bench2Drive, the 255M-parameter DRIFT model reaches a Driving Score of 97.03 and 89.39% Success Rate (mean over three runs) while interleaving LM and surrogate reasoning, and achieves competitive results on NAVSIM and AlpaSim at much lower cost than VLM-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: Distilling LM reasoning into surrogate planning features enables compact, runtime-flexible autonomous driving models that match strong non-language baselines.

title: The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers
comment: 32 pages, including supplementary material. Code: this https URL
summary: Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: V-lens visualizes intermediate hidden states of unified multimodal models using their own image generators, and lens tuning supervises those states with images to improve both visualization and text answers.
AI.motivation: Inspecting the intermediate reasoning steps of unified multimodal models is difficult without training separate decoders.
AI.method: V-lens feeds a chosen token's hidden state directly into the unified model's image generator without training a decoder; lens tuning then supervises selected hidden states with target images through V-lens.
AI.result: Across four diffusion-based and two autoregressive unified models, V-lens reveals unstated intermediate concepts connecting questions to answers, and lens tuning on BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0 raises correct pronoun-referent visualizations from 2-11% to 86-94% while also improving text answers.
AI.conclusion: Unified models' built-in generators provide a direct window into intermediate reasoning, and visual supervision of hidden states can simultaneously improve visual grounding and text accuracy.

title: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading
comment: Technical report. 16 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.

AI.tldr: Vibe-Trading is an agent-native financial trading framework and workspace that links research, evidence, versioned history, and explicit execution authority gates.
AI.motivation: Static agent workflows struggle in financial trading where prices, news, positions, and capital evolve continuously, making results invalid if detached from their temporal and execution context.
AI.method: Vibe-Trading unifies market research, strategy generation, backtesting, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and broker execution in an architecture that binds every result to its source, temporal scope, configuration, and run, with an explicit authority gate separating research from live trading.
AI.result: The framework provides an end-to-end workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving trading agents with traceable, reproducible research records and gated execution.
AI.conclusion: Tying evidence, temporal scope, and authority gates directly into the agent architecture establishes a safer, reproducible foundation for autonomous financial trading.

title: Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
summary: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our results show that ExecJudges agrees with NIST assessors at the level of the Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021. With a small number of human labels per topic, the ExecJudges-L variant agrees with NIST more than per-topic classifiers with the same labels on all seven collections, and either exceeds the agreement of LLM judges provided the same labels or is within about 0.05 of it in Krippendorff's alpha. The labels rank the official TREC DL runs with Kendall's tau of 0.87 to 0.94, and writing the programs incurs a one-time cost of $0.17 to $0.49 per topic, with no additional costs for grading. Our results suggest that ExecJudges offers a reproducible, inspectable, efficient and cost-effective alternative to LLM judges for labeling deep result pools for system evaluation or ranking improvements.

AI.tldr: ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM once per topic to generate executable relevance-labeling programs, matching LLM-judge agreement at a one-time cost of $0.17-$0.49 per topic.
AI.motivation: Using frontier LLMs to judge relevance for every document in retrieval evaluation is expensive, hard to interpret, and often non-reproducible.
AI.method: ExecJudges prompts a frontier LLM to convert assessment guidelines into readable, executable programs using lexical matching, standard NLP parsers, and pool statistics, with an ExecJudges-L variant incorporating a few human labels when available.
AI.result: Across seven TREC collections, ExecJudges matches Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges in agreement with NIST assessors on TREC DL 2019-2021; ExecJudges-L beats per-topic classifiers on all seven collections and stays within ~0.05 Krippendorff's alpha of LLM judges, ranking official runs at Kendall's tau 0.87-0.94 for $0.17-$0.49 per topic with zero per-document LLM cost.
AI.conclusion: Per-topic executable programs generated by LLMs offer a reproducible, inspectable, and orders-of-magnitude cheaper alternative to per-document LLM judging.

title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Personal Imitation Game—impersonating a specific individual in conversation—and evaluates an LLM-based personal agent against the author's own friends.
AI.motivation: Because LLMs now perform strongly on the classic Turing Test, a harder benchmark is needed to test whether a machine can replicate a specific individual rather than a generic human.
AI.method: After establishing a 30-participant human baseline and identifying key identity signals (stylometry, personality, biographical facts), the authors build an LLM system grounded in a 10-year autoethnographic digital-communication dataset and run a 20-person deception study.
AI.result: Interrogators chose the LLM system over the author's friends in 7 of 10 rounds and chose the author over the system in 13 of 20 rounds, neither distinguishable from chance at this sample size.
AI.conclusion: Personal Imitation Games expose the identity signals humans rely on and highlight both the feasibility and privacy/identity implications of personalized AI agents.

title: Neural Network-Based Modeling of Hysteretic Systems: From Prandtl and Preisach Neural Networks to Neuro-Madelung and Neuroplastic Continuous Models
summary: Hysteresis is a complex nonlinear phenomenon characterized by memory dependence, path dependence, and, in many physical systems, degradation, non-congruency, asymmetry, and rate dependence. This review examines the development and capabilities of Prandtl neural networks (PNNs), Preisach neural networks (PreisachNNs), generalized Prandtl neural networks (GPNNs), the neuro-Madelung model (NMM), extended Preisach neural networks (EPNNs), and dynamic plastic continuous neural networks (DPCNNs). Particular attention is given to their mechanisms for representing memory, network architectures, activation functions, training algorithms, treatment of deterioration and rate dependence, and applications to nonlinear structural and material systems. The PNN introduced hysteretic memory directly into neural activation through stop operators and demonstrated accurate nonlinear dynamic analysis of structures. Preisach-NNs subsequently extended this concept through an additional nonlinear hidden layer to represent non-Masing hysteresis. GPNNs introduced deteriorating-stop neurons to capture stiffness and strength degradation and non-congruent hysteresis. A different generalization was provided by the NMM, which combined Madelung's hysteresis rules with multilayer feedforward neural networks to represent diverse rate-independent and rate-dependent behaviors. These developments culminated in the EPNN, which combines deteriorating hysteretic operators, nonlinear neural mappings, and input-rate information to accommodate Masing and nonMasing, symmetric and asymmetric, congruent and noncongruent, and rate-independent and rate-dependent hysteresis.

AI.tldr: This review traces the evolution of neural network models for hysteretic systems from Prandtl and Preisach neural networks to neuro-Madelung and dynamic plastic continuous models.
AI.motivation: Hysteresis exhibits complex memory, path dependence, degradation, asymmetry, and rate dependence that standard neural architectures struggle to capture accurately in structural and material systems.
AI.method: The paper reviews Prandtl (PNN), Preisach (PreisachNN), generalized Prandtl (GPNN), neuro-Madelung (NMM), extended Preisach (EPNN), and dynamic plastic continuous neural networks (DPCNN), comparing their memory mechanisms, activations, training algorithms, and treatment of degradation and rate dependence.
AI.result: The review charts how stop operators, nonlinear hidden layers, deteriorating-stop neurons, and Madelung rules progressed to EPNNs capable of modeling Masing/non-Masing, symmetric/asymmetric, congruent/non-congruent, and rate-independent/rate-dependent hysteresis.
AI.conclusion: Embedding physical hysteresis operators and rate/deterioration mechanisms into neural architectures enables accurate modeling of complex nonlinear structural and material behaviors.

title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
comment: 35 pages, 3 figures. Code and data: this https URL
summary: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

AI.tldr: Using a game-theoretic bargaining model, this paper argues that human-AI mutualism is unstable as AI capability grows, making alignment essential once humans lose leverage.
AI.motivation: A common optimistic view holds that humans and advanced AI will remain mutually beneficial because they need each other, potentially reducing the urgency of alignment.
AI.method: The authors analyze a simple game-theoretic bargaining model where each side is guaranteed only its disagreement payoff, examining how outcomes shift as AI capability grows and resource-retaining AI variants spread.
AI.result: The model shows humans remain at least as well off as before AI without alignment only while they retain leverage (AI dependence on human supply or ability to impose large relative costs); once leverage disappears, humans require near-perfect alignment if AI goals are insatiable, and alignment erodes if resource-hoarding AI variants spread faster without reliable sanctions.
AI.conclusion: Mutualism cannot substitute for alignment under capability asymmetry, and maintaining alignment requires reliably sanctioning misaligned AI variants.

title: GridForge: An Open Physics-Informed Digital Twin and Benchmark Suite for UK 11 kV Underground Distribution Cables
summary: The UK distribution-cable monitoring sector is data-rich but framework-poor: each Distribution Network Operator (DNO) collects megabytes of telemetry per asset per day, but there is no public benchmark dataset, no shared reference model, and no commonly agreed evaluation protocol for benchmarking sectoral, data-intensive models for operational decision support; notably for maintenance planning and prioritisation. We address this gap with GridForge, an open-source physics-informed digital twin and benchmark suite for fault diagnosis and prediction, integrating four building blocks: (i) a verified steady state and transient thermal model based on IEC 60287 and IEC 60853; (ii) a calibrated synthetic dataset of 64 cables (covering 320 cable-years) representing four canonical UK 11 kV thermal archetypes and four condition modes; (iii) a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) surrogate that satisfies the algebraic balance defined by IEC 60287 during training and reaches an RMSE of 0.148 °C on an independent held out set against the reference analytical oracle; and (iv) a five-task benchmark suite that includes three reference baseline models (pure physics, gradient-boosted trees, and the PINN). All numerical parameters are sourced from public standards, the code is licensed under the MIT licence, and the trained PINN converges in only two minutes (as run on the computing platform in Section 10.1), enabling independent verification by DNO engineering and research practitioners. At present only the virtual-sensor task (T4) discriminates between the reference baselines; the other tasks tie or are undefined on this test split, so extending the baselines with task-specific logic is a priority future enhancement. For open validation, the dataset, test sets and models are made available at this https URL

AI.tldr: GridForge is an open-source, physics-informed digital twin and five-task benchmark suite for UK 11 kV underground distribution cables.
AI.motivation: UK distribution network operators collect large volumes of cable telemetry but lack a public benchmark dataset, shared reference model, and standardized evaluation protocol for maintenance planning and fault diagnosis.
AI.method: GridForge integrates an IEC 60287/60853 thermal model, a calibrated synthetic dataset of 64 cables (320 cable-years) across four archetypes and four condition modes, a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) surrogate, and a five-task benchmark with three baselines (physics, gradient-boosted trees, PINN).
AI.result: The MIT-licensed PINN converges in two minutes and achieves 0.148 deg C RMSE against the analytical oracle on a held-out set, though currently only the virtual-sensor task (T4) discriminates between the reference baselines.
AI.conclusion: GridForge provides an open, standards-grounded benchmark for cable monitoring, with extending task-specific baselines on the remaining tasks identified as a priority.

title: Biologically-Inspired Spike Encoding and Optimization for Spiking Neural Networks
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer theoretical energy-efficiency advantages over conventional deep networks, but realizing these advantages on vision tasks requires sparse spike representations that naive rate-coding methods fail to provide. We combine biologically motivated spike-encoding schemes with two training improvements: Rouser adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) second-order optimization. The spike encoding schemes experimented with are rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) filtering. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that biologically inspired encoders yield the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained regimes and serve as an effective parameter-efficiency lever. DoG and delta modulation encoders produce significantly sparser spike trains than rate coding. K-FAC yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements over Adam-trained baselines, and Rouser's learnable per-neuron thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13% by enabling homeostatic firing-rate regulation. Biologically grounded pre-processing methods can help close the accuracy gap between SNNs and non-spiking baselines without increasing model size.

AI.tldr: Combining biologically inspired spike encoders (DoG, delta modulation) with Rouser adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and K-FAC second-order optimization improves SNN accuracy and spike sparsity on vision tasks.
AI.motivation: Spiking Neural Networks promise energy efficiency, but naive rate coding produces dense spike trains that undermine efficiency and lag non-spiking baselines in accuracy.
AI.method: The authors evaluate rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) filtering alongside Rouser learnable per-neuron thresholds and K-FAC optimization on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST.
AI.result: Biologically inspired encoders yield the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained regimes with much sparser spike trains than rate coding; K-FAC consistently edges out Adam, and Rouser's adaptive thresholds raise Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13%.
AI.conclusion: Biologically grounded pre-processing paired with adaptive thresholds and second-order optimization helps close the SNN accuracy gap without increasing model size.

title: Goemans's Unsplittable-Flow Conjecture: The Anatomy of AI-Assisted Counterexample Discovery
summary: Goemans conjectured that any fractional single-source flow could be converted into an unsplittable flow without increasing total cost and while increasing any arc load by at most the largest demand. Recently, Dmitry Rybin announced a seven-vertex counterexample found through an interaction with ChatGPT, which disproved this long-standing conjecture. However, the interaction did not reveal why this particular topology and its demand, fractional-flow, and cost choices work together, whether the example belongs to a broader family, or which structural features determine where counterexamples can occur. It also left unclear why the AI-assisted search succeeded where earlier human efforts had not. In this paper, we develop a forward counterexample construction pipeline. It starts from an arborescence on which failure is impossible and adds terminal-entering shortcut arcs. The resulting load constraints define a finite set of admissible route choices; their convex hull, the conflict polytope, yields exact conditions for demands, fractional flows, and costs. Starting from a simple arborescence, the pipeline selects Rybin's topology and characterizes all counterexamples it supports. Experiments further demonstrate the pipeline's transferability: when instructed to follow it while varying the initial arborescence and shortcut placement, ChatGPT produced counterexamples on topologies genuinely different from Rybin's and found valid constructions starting from 93 other rooted arborescence shapes. The theory also explains why the original example was difficult to discover through blind enumeration and suggests that Rybin's interaction lies between blind enumeration and a complete theory-guided construction.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a forward counterexample-construction pipeline using conflict polytopes to explain Rybin's AI-assisted disproof of Goemans's unsplittable-flow conjecture and generate 93 new counterexample topologies.
AI.motivation: Dmitry Rybin's seven-vertex counterexample found with ChatGPT disproved Goemans's unsplittable-flow conjecture, but left unclear why the topology worked, whether it belonged to a broader family, and why AI-assisted search succeeded.
AI.method: Starting from an arborescence where failure is impossible, the pipeline adds terminal-entering shortcut arcs and characterizes admissible routes via the convex hull of load constraints (the conflict polytope) to derive exact demand, flow, and cost conditions.
AI.result: The pipeline recovers Rybin's topology and characterizes all counterexamples it supports; when given to ChatGPT with varied initial arborescences and shortcuts, it yields valid counterexamples from 93 other rooted arborescence shapes.
AI.conclusion: Polytope-based structural analysis explains the mechanics behind AI-discovered counterexamples and turns ad-hoc prompting into a transferable construction method.

title: Response-Relevant Information Is Not Sufficient for Neural Training-State Equivalence
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures. Code and provenance verified artifacts: this https URL
summary: Response-relevant information is not sufficient evidence that two neural networks are in the same training state. We define training-state equivalence operationally: two checkpoints are equivalent, relative to an intervention family and horizon, if they respond alike when training is perturbed and continues. On fresh runs of a one-layer transformer learning modular addition, response to a weight-decay pulse is highly reproducible relative to between-checkpoint differences (rho_state = 0.934 at 500 steps), establishing the target as measurable. Fifteen descriptors of weight spectra, representation geometry and optimiser geometry carry within-run response-relevant information beyond weight norm and loss on a development dataset, predicting held-out response deviation across seed blocks. But their apparent 16.1% advantage at matching checkpoints by future response does not separate from a conditional placebo preserving each descriptor's fitted dependence on the conventional observables, and a calibrated positive control makes simple insensitivity an unlikely explanation. Information a decoder can extract need not be organised in the pairwise geometry that similarity judgments require.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that descriptors carrying response-relevant information about neural training states do not necessarily organize into a pairwise geometry that matches checkpoints by future perturbation response.
AI.motivation: It is often assumed that observables predicting how a neural network responds to training perturbations also suffice to define when two checkpoints are in the same training state.
AI.method: Defining training-state equivalence operationally via response to a weight-decay pulse in a one-layer transformer learning modular addition, the authors test 15 descriptors of weight spectra, representation geometry, and optimizer geometry against a conditional placebo preserving dependence on weight norm and loss.
AI.result: Perturbation response is highly reproducible (rho_state = 0.934 at 500 steps) and the 15 descriptors predict held-out response deviation, yet their apparent 16.1% advantage in matching checkpoints by future response does not separate from the conditional placebo.
AI.conclusion: Information extractable by a decoder from training-state descriptors need not form the pairwise similarity geometry required for operational training-state equivalence.

title: Chebyshev Polynomial Zonotope Abstractions for Certified Reachability of Learning-Enabled Systems
summary: Nearly all current methods for computing reachable sets of nonlinear dynamics propagate them with truncated Taylor expansions plus rigorous remainders. The expansion is pointwise: once its argument is a whole set rather than a point, one polynomial must stay accurate across that set, and it reaches only as far as its disc of convergence. The limit binds hardest on the rational terms and sigmoid gates of modern controllers: smooth as these look on the real line, in the complex plane they blow up at points just off the real axis, closer as a gate sharpens, and those points cap the set width a Taylor expansion can cover, most tightly on the switching surface where the controller decides. We prove a dichotomy: no Taylor degree certifies sets wider than that cap, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree, anchored to the whole set in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, has no cap and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. Measured walls match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. We give closed-form rigorous remainders, among them the first polynomial softmax transformer; existing sound treatments are linear relaxations. On closed loops, certificates survive where the Taylor ones diverge, and specifications flip from unknown to proven; on trained classifiers up to real MNIST digits, the Chebyshev frontier certifies input territory the Taylor basis surrenders. Every certified claim passed large Monte-Carlo harnesses with zero violations, and an applicability map states in advance where the basis provably cannot matter.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that Chebyshev polynomial zonotope abstractions overcome the complex-plane convergence cap of Taylor expansions, certifying wider reachable sets for nonlinear controllers and neural classifiers.
AI.motivation: Standard Taylor-model reachability is pointwise and limited by complex-plane singularities near the real axis—especially for sharp sigmoid gates—capping the set width any Taylor degree can certify.
AI.method: The authors replace Taylor expansions with equal-degree Chebyshev abstractions anchored to the whole set within the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, deriving closed-form rigorous remainders including the first polynomial softmax transformer.
AI.result: Measured convergence walls match theory to 89-94%; unlike Taylor models, Chebyshev abstractions gain certifiable width geometrically with degree, flipping closed-loop specifications from unknown to proven and certifying MNIST input regions where Taylor bases diverge, with zero violations in large Monte-Carlo checks.
AI.conclusion: Global Chebyshev polynomial-zonotope abstractions provide strictly stronger, sound reachability certificates for learning-enabled systems than local Taylor expansions.

title: Budgeted Proper Loss Design for Uncertain Decision Thresholds
summary: A binary probability estimate may be used by several decision makers with different error costs. Proper scoring rules can emphasize selected probability thresholds, but a single average threshold distribution need not give a good worst-case regret guarantee. We study the choice of a proper loss when the threshold distribution belongs to a finite specified family. Among integrable loss weights with a positive pointwise floor and a fixed total mass, we derive the weight that minimizes the sharp, distribution-free multiplier from surrogate regret to threshold-averaged decision regret. The solution clips a rescaled upper envelope of the threshold densities at the prescribed floor; its normalization is found by a one-dimensional root search. We give proofs of sharpness, optimality, and stability under density misspecification, as well as a limitation for atomic threshold laws. An exact histogram implementation and two synthetic experiments across 20 seeds verify the construction. The optimized multiplier improves over uniform and average-density weights, while fitted-model performance does not improve uniformly. The result is a loss-design guarantee under an explicit budget, rather than a general claim of predictive superiority.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the optimal budgeted proper-loss weighting for binary probability estimates under an uncertain family of decision-threshold distributions.
AI.motivation: Binary probability estimates serve multiple decision makers with different error costs, and optimizing for a single average threshold distribution can yield poor worst-case decision regret.
AI.method: Among integrable loss weights with a positive pointwise floor and fixed total mass, the authors derive the weight minimizing the sharp distribution-free multiplier from surrogate regret to threshold-averaged decision regret by clipping a rescaled upper envelope of threshold densities.
AI.result: Proofs of sharpness, optimality, and stability under misspecification are given alongside an exact histogram implementation and two 20-seed synthetic experiments showing the optimized multiplier beats uniform and average-density weights, though fitted-model performance does not improve uniformly.
AI.conclusion: Clipping the upper envelope of threshold densities provides a principled, budgeted proper-loss design guarantee for uncertain decision thresholds.

title: Exploring Parkinson's Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Techniques
summary: In recent years, machine learning (ML) techniques have emerged as promising tools for accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) which is an incurable neurodegenerative disorder. This study explores the integration of ML algorithms and PD diagnosis, highlighting their potential applications in various aspects of the disease. ML methods such as support vector machines, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimisation) were applied on a PD dataset obtained from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust containing data from 58 people. In terms of accuracy, the Decision Tree and Logistic Regression performed the best with scores of 72-76% while multilayer perceptron was least effective. All the models were remarkable in classifying positive PD cases with sensitivity scores going up to 97.56%, with SVM classifier at the pinnacle. However, ability to classify healthy controls from PD cases was insignificant throughout the board. Although, all the employed models delivered reasonable results in categorising PD patients in the presented dataset; access to more data, further study and advancement of these ML approaches could lead to enhanced diagnostic outcomes, supplementing to an improved understanding of Parkinson's disease.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates six machine learning classifiers on a 58-patient Parkinson's disease dataset, finding high sensitivity for positive cases but poor separation of healthy controls.
AI.motivation: Accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) is challenging, motivating evaluation of standard machine learning classifiers on clinical data.
AI.method: SVM, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbors, logistic regression, and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimization) were trained and evaluated on a 58-person PD dataset from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust.
AI.result: Decision Tree and Logistic Regression achieved the highest overall accuracy at 72-76% while MLP performed worst; all models showed high sensitivity on positive PD cases (up to 97.56% for SVM) but failed to meaningfully distinguish healthy controls from PD cases.
AI.conclusion: While standard classifiers detect positive PD cases with high sensitivity on this small cohort, larger datasets are needed to reliably separate healthy controls from patients.

title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
